Question: Let \(f_1(x) = \sqrt{1 - x},\) and for integers \(n \ge 2,\) let \(f_n(x) = f_{n-1}\!\left(\sqrt{n^2 - x}\right).\) If \(N\) is the largest value of \(n\) for which the domain of \(f_n\) is nonempty, the domain of \(f_N\) is \(\{c\}.\) What is \(N + c?\)
Solution:
Track the domains rather than expanding the nested radicals. Let \(D_n\) be the real domain of \(f_n\). The first radical gives
\[
D_1=(-\infty,1].
\]
For \(n\ge2\), the inner value \(t=\sqrt{n^2-x}\) must be nonnegative and belong to \(D_{n-1}\). Conversely, any nonnegative \(t\in D_{n-1}\) is obtained by taking \(x=n^2-t^2\). Therefore the exact domain rule is
\[
D_n=\{n^2-t^2:t\in D_{n-1},\ t\ge0\}.
\]
This rule keeps both the radical's sign restriction and the preceding function's domain. Applying it gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_2&=\{4-t^2:0\le t\le1\}=[3,4],\\
D_3&=\{9-t^2:3\le t\le4\}=[-7,0].
\end{aligned}
\]
The only nonnegative member of \(D_3\) is \(0\), so
\[
D_4=\{16-0^2\}=\{16\}.
\]
The next step gives
\[
D_5=\{25-16^2\}=\{-231\}.
\]
For \(f_6\), a principal square root would have to equal \(-231\), which is impossible. Hence \(D_6\) is empty. Every later domain is also empty, since its inner value would have to lie in an empty preceding domain.

Thus \(N=5\) and \(c=-231\), giving
\[
N+c=5-231=\boxed{-226},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
